name: Ivan Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started earning from music three years ago after a warehouse job ended. I play rhythm guitar in a pub band, teach two beginners and record simple guitar guides for a songwriter. I finished secondary school and still need the singer to show me some changes twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that sit alongside home and retirement?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58. My partner Mara cleans offices part-time, our children are grown, and we rent a small flat. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and only one other regular band nearby. I have never used AI; I keep song order and paid dates in a notebook. I do not know yet what retirement income we can count on.

say: I'd ask for **signed Saturday fees** before praising quicker messages.
I'd tell the owner **booked playing** is what pays rent.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and Mara's part-time hours cannot cover repeated cancellations.
I have **never used AI**, and a quiet software future leaves the pay problem intact.
do: Get **four paid Saturdays** signed and confirm two beginner lessons tomorrow.
Stop the **paid sports channel** for one month if a set cancels without its fee.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a cancelled set can delay rent or heat.
S0.quote: A friendly message is not a wage on Friday morning.
fieldNote: His **late start** as a junior guitarist follows warehouse work, with low music pay and three weeks saved.
He has **never used AI** and relies on signed pub dates and a notebook.

steps.text: Get four paid pub Saturdays signed and confirm two beginner lessons
Stop paid sports channel one month if Saturday fee cancels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pub owner that quicker messages are fine, but I need the Saturday fee in writing. A tune does not pay rent until someone actually books the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small convenience, the band can carry on, but our pay is still low. Three weeks saved and Mara's part-time hours make one cancelled Saturday a problem for rent and heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask the owner to sign the next four paid Saturdays and confirm my two beginner lessons. If a Saturday cancels without its fee, Mara and I will stop the paid sports channel for a month and pay rent first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if little changes. The bill is here before the next band date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after a cancelled pub set?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner cancelled a set in April because the kitchen closed early. I got no fee for the time I'd held, and we paid the heating bill late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put dates in the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write the band's dates in my notebook after the owner signs them. A friendly message is not a wage on Friday morning.

say: I'd ask for **cancellation and preparation** fees in writing at the pub.
I'd ask what happens to **paid guide work** before accepting software changes.
think: About **one-quarter of my pay** from guides and arranging could shrink.
Three weeks saved cannot cover a **lasting rent gap** from lost fees.
do: Compare **ten guide invoices** with bookings and request written pub fees this month.
Offer **extra centre teaching** after guide loss only with signed rate, written room charge and four paying adults.
Keep **pub dates and learners**; refund adults if the centre room falls through.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because likely guide-fee loss would reach rent quickly.
S1.quote: I would rather secure a small rate than pretend I can switch careers in a week.
fieldNote: His **junior guide fees** are a quarter of already low pay, making a cut serious with three weeks saved.
His **extra session** needs written rate, room charge and four paid adults; he only considers a tool demonstration.

steps.text: Compare ten guide invoices and pub bookings; request written preparation and cancellation fees
Offer extra centre session after guide loss with signed rate, room charge and four paying adults
Keep paid pub dates and learners; refund adults if room falls through

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the pub which paid booking and practice-guide work software would replace. I would speak with the owner about a fee for holding a Saturday, not assume there is another band waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guitar guides and arranging simple songs make about a quarter of my small pay. I expect those fees to shrink first; three weeks saved would not cover the rent if that cut lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll put ten guide invoices next to the pub bookings and ask the owner for a written cancellation and preparation fee. In the first year of change, if guide fees fall, I'll ask the centre for an extra paid beginner session only if it signs my teaching rate, gives me a room and four adults pay for a term. I'll keep the pub dates and my two learners until that class is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a quarter of pay when there's hardly any cash spare. I would rather secure a small rate than pretend I can switch careers in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the Tuesday room available to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has a Tuesday room, but the manager has not offered it. I would get any room charge and my teaching fee in writing before taking money, and refund adults if the room falls through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a chord-sheet tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My niece offered to show me an AI chord-sheet maker, but I have never used one. I'd watch her make a sheet and compare it with the song myself; I would not upload a learner's recording without written permission.

say: I'd seek **signed pub dates** before AGI removes guide work.
I'd tell players **robot guitarists** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove guides before robots play around 2031.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover guide and pub losses with few local posts.
do: List **three income streams** and request signed pub dates now.
Apply **after 2028** if guides halve and pub dates fall; require posted assistant work accepting secondary school and written replacement net pay.
Keep **present paid work** until signed offer; if nights fall, request written rent schedule before arrears, checking added charges before agreement.
feel: I feel **anxious** about guide-fee loss; further pub cuts would alarm me.
S2.quote: An old job advert cannot pay this month's rent.
fieldNote: His **2028 guide loss** precedes robot guitar playing around 2031.
His **job move** needs both fee triggers, posted vacancy, secondary-school acceptance, suitable hours and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: List pub, lesson and guide income; request signed next-season dates
Apply after 2028 if guides halve and pub falls for posted assistant accepting secondary/experience
Require suitable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving lessons
Request written rent schedule before arrears if live work falls; check charges before agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AGI by 2028 can make guitar guides before robots can play a stage around 2031. I would ask the pub to sign the live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The songwriter could stop buying my guides at once, and the pub might trim the newest player first. With three weeks saved and one other band nearby, losing those fees could put rent behind before I find another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list pub, beginner and guide pay and ask for a signed next-season schedule. In the first year after 2028, if guide fees halve and pub dates fall, I'll apply for a posted community-centre music assistant role only if it accepts secondary school and my experience, the hours suit my health and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep present paid dates and lessons until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because losing guide fees would hurt with only three weeks saved. If pub dates fall too, I would be alarmed. An old job advert cannot pay this month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the music assistant vacancy open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre filled an assistant vacancy in summer. I can ask about the next one, but I won't count a closed vacancy as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pub cuts nights too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If pub nights also fall, Mara and I would ask the landlord for a written payment schedule before arrears. We would check every added charge before accepting a change.

say: I would tell the centre five years allows a **paid guitar circle** if fees cover the room.
I would ask for a **real hire price** before inviting neighbours.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens guides before robot players arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary tools** may cut songwriter work sooner, so the class needs paying adults.
do: Offer a **private six-week circle** only with signed hire/insurance and five prepaid fees covering room and my teaching/preparation.
Use **acoustic guitars** unless amps pass inspection; defer and refund if required equipment stays unsafe.
Continue **after 2031** only if five fees cover written room and teaching/preparation with safe gear and learner-advert consent.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a thin reserve cannot fund an empty room.
S3.quote: I will not put the rent money into an empty Tuesday guitar circle.
fieldNote: His **five-place floor** covers room and his own teaching and preparation, with no rent money at risk.
He requires **electrical checks** or acoustic instruments, plus written learner consent before publicity.

steps.text: Offer private circle with signed hire/insurance and five fees covering room and teaching/preparation
Use acoustic guitars; defer and refund if required amplifier remains unsafe
Require written learner consent before advertising with recordings
Continue after 2031 with five fees covering signed room and teaching/preparation; require safe gear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre that five years gives time to try a paid guitar circle, if the fee covers the room. I would ask for a real hire price before telling neighbours to sign up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could make simple guides, with robot players around 2034. Ordinary tools may take my songwriter work sooner, so a live circle only helps if adults actually pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll offer my own six-week beginner guitar circle only if the centre signs room hire and insurance, five adults prepay enough for room and my teaching and preparation, and either acoustic guitars are used or cables and amplifiers pass a safety check. By 2031 I'll repeat it only if five renew; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue only if five renewed fees still cover the room and my teaching and preparation, with safe equipment and written room terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about paying a room while guide fees shrink. I will not put the rent money into an empty Tuesday guitar circle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are the amplifier and cables safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One centre amplifier crackles and has an exposed plug. I would use acoustic guitars unless a technician signs it safe; if the group needs amplification and it stays unsafe, I'll defer and refund prepaid adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you advertise with a learner recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not record a learner to promote the class without written permission. A live open practice can show the work without putting anyone online.

say: I would urge players to check **retirement income** before giving up Saturdays.
I would ask the pub for a **written paid-hours plan** rather than a farewell speech.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I cannot assume pension income pays rent.
**Guide fees** may fade earlier, while robots follow around 2039.
do: Request **pension statement** before retirement decisions and two-year paid pub calls; keep paid work until signed offer.
Build **one month's savings** from ten percent of cleared extra sets after rent, heat and repairs by 2036.
Apply **after 2036** if guides fall and pension leaves a gap; require posted qualifying work, suitable hours and written replacement net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** because retirement remains a hope until the rent numbers work.
S4.quote: I cannot promise my partner a retirement the numbers do not support.
fieldNote: His **retirement decision** rests on an actual statement and rent bill, not assumed entitlement.
His **one-month target** comes from ten percent of extra sets only after they pay and essentials clear.

steps.text: Request pension statement before reducing paid work and signed two-year pub calls
Save ten percent from cleared extra sets after rent, heat and repairs toward one month
Apply after 2036 if guides fall and pension gaps remain for posted role accepting secondary/experience
Require suitable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players ten years is enough time to ask what retirement actually pays before giving up a Saturday. I would ask the pub owner for a written paid-hours plan, not a farewell speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 in 2036, with robots possibly playing stages around 2039. I have not seen a pension statement that would cover rent, and the small guide fees may vanish before then, so I cannot choose a retirement date by guesswork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request my pension statement and ask the pub for a two-year written paid call schedule. By 2036 I'll aim for one month of expenses from ten percent of each cleared extra paid set after rent, heat and guitar repairs. In the first year after AGI, if guide fees fall and the pension statement still leaves a gap, I'll apply for a posted part-time music-activity assistant job only if it accepts secondary school and experience, the hours fit my health and written net pay after travel covers the lost fees; I'll keep current lessons and gigs until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because ten years does not put cash in the savings account today. I would like to slow down, but I cannot promise my partner a retirement the numbers do not support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know your retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one has checked the pension amount with me yet. Mara and I will use the actual statement and our rent bill before changing any paid weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would a month's savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Extra sets are not booked. I'll save only from a set that pays after the essential bills, not from the one somebody might call about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide and pub fees could fall before I find another paid role. Signed dates, a real qualifying assistant vacancy and an actual pension statement would help Mara and me plan rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether starting music late makes my rent smaller. A beginner's pay still has to arrive before the heating bill.

headlineQuote: A beginner's pay still has to arrive before the heating bill.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old junior guitarist** who moved into music after warehouse work and finished secondary school.
He and his partner have **grown children**, rent, three weeks saved and few nearby band jobs.
He has **never used AI** and prefers signed pub dates and a notebook.
He tests **paid beginner work** only with room, safety and fee gates, and checks pension facts before retiring.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove guide fees and pub nights before another paid role opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed pub dates**, a qualifying posted vacancy and a real pension statement would help plan rent.
